narratives.common: Most groups describe the 2026 US midterms as a sweeping Democratic win, often called a 'blue wave' or 'sweep'. Democrats flipped dozens of House seats and made gains in state legislatures, while some Senate races, such as Mississippi and Alaska, were still being counted. Coverage turns to what Democrats will do with their new power and how President Trump will respond.

groups.distinct: Posts are short and scattershot. They cover Elon Musk's near-half-billion-dollar spending with little return, a reported congressional 'investigative blitz' into Apple, Meta and Musk's companies, and Canada's Carney welcoming a push to repeal the tariffs. Others celebrate Crystalyne Curley's election as first woman Navajo Nation president and a DSA post claiming voters 'endorsed socialism'. Some are celebratory or humorous (Jane Fonda, Russell Howard) and some share maps.

Barely addresses the results. Commenters argue about voter ID and Trump's election-related moves, and link to coverage of court rejections. They also bring in tangents such as Ukraine, the Iran war and its effect on midterm prospects, wind power and local Napa Valley politics. One user shares a data dashboard on congressional control.

Focuses on local and state results: a Washington House supermajority, Democrats taking the Texas House and State Board of Education, and reactions from Rochester voters. It also covers the lame-duck session, business implications and whether young voters who backed Democrats will stay with them. Close Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska and Boebert trailing in Colorado are mentioned.

Stresses the aftermath: market and business effects (a Wall Street selloff, Iran war escalation risk despite the sweep), and the surprise even Democrats' House super PAC felt at the wave's size. It also looks ahead to what Democrats will do with state power and to 2028 being 'an open question'. Specific coverage includes lists of flipped districts, with more than 40 House flips counted.

outlet_notes: Brennan Center for Justice: left (AI estimate)
The New York Times: center-left (AI estimate)
groups.distinct: Gives data and institutional detail: charts on the wave's scope, Brennan Center analysis of surprising turnout, and the Mississippi Senate lead growing. It also covers Trump signaling he is ready to 'battle' the Democratic majority, Rep. Clark as likely House Majority Leader, and a Kansas GOP supermajority broken. The Washington Post describes a 'slim' House majority as favored, a narrower framing than others.

Takes an analytic, international view. It uses sweeping language such as 'the mother of all American course corrections' and 'historic', and frames results around populism, the future of both parties and 2028. It also offers takeaways from an event and how Democrats will wield power.

Reads the results through India's interests: effects on Indian students and workers, what a Democratic sweep means for 'Trump, India and the world', and US power. WION puts the Democratic count near 260 seats and says it would be the biggest House majority since 1991.

Emphasizes foreign policy and markets: a Democratic win may shift Trump's focus abroad, the 'anti-AI trade' lifting Indian and Chinese stocks, and why Delhi should engage 'the many Americas'. NDTV describes a Democratic majority 'since 2008' and calls it a 'rout' for Trump.

conflicts: WION (Indian media) says Democrats are poised for their biggest House majority since 1991, while NDTV (Indian media, centrist) says since 2008.
The Washington Post (US media, left-leaning) says Democrats are favored to win a 'slim' House majority, while WION (Indian media) says they are closing in on about 260 seats, a historic majority.

narrative:
Coverage of the 2026 US midterms splits across five framings, though only 51 of 160 items (32%) carried one. The divide is rated strong (kappa 0.58).

The largest framing, live results and vote tracking (33%), presents tallies, maps and charts with little interpretation. In the headline evidence it appears from Reuters, NBC News, Bloomberg, the Financial Times and CBS News. Republican and Trump fallout (29%) frames the result as a rebuke and a source of turmoil. It appears in headlines from PBS, AP, MS NOW, CNN and The Telegraph, and in posts from mastodon:killbait. Voter blocs and long-term shifts (16%) shows up at The Washington Post, The Conversation, CNN and SBS. Markets and business (12%) appears at the Financial Times, Bloomberg, CNBC and The Japan Times' Mastodon account. Democratic mandate and governing agenda (10%) is the smallest, with CBS News, SBS and mastodon:DrALJONES as examples.

Several outlets span more than one framing. Bloomberg, CNN and the FT each appear in two.

Limits: every outlet and account is still marked "building," with only 1 to 4 outlet items and 1 to 13 account items each. Outlet leanings are inferred from headlines and snippets, and the data supplies no lean labels. Sample sizes are small.

narratives.common: Opposition to data centers has grown into a visible political and protest movement. US midterm results are widely described as a voter rebuke tied to data center and AI expansion, with tech firms such as OpenAI and Meta responding. Protests have also spread to Europe, including an incident in which activists entered a Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam.

groups.distinct: Commenters debate causes rather than report events. They offer explanations such as anger over gas and grocery prices, hostility to AI itself rather than to data centers, and tech industry 'arrogant, high-handed' siting with NDAs and 'suborned' local governments. Some suggest pitching renewables on cost predictability, and others argue the industry did foresee the backlash, citing secrecy and space data centers.

Headlines are corporate and local in focus: Nvidia's plan to retrofit Apollo's old phone buildings, OpenAI's efforts to ease backlash, and Georgia as an 'underappreciated risk'. They also cover the protest outside Schumer's Brooklyn home and protests in France and Spain.

Stresses market and policy consequences: an Anthropic IPO facing backlash, energy stocks hit by a 'blue wave', and expectations of tougher regulation. It also reports Big Tech's claim that the vote was 'anti-Trump' rather than 'anti-tech'.

outlets: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
outlet_notes: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos: center-left (AI estimate)
American Civil Liberties Union: left (AI estimate)

groups.distinct: Gives more local and partisan detail: Democrats using anger over data centers to flip red states, incumbents ousted in Minnesota towns, and Schumer's 'dirty data center deal' under protest. It adds a civil rights and civil liberties framing (ACLU) and Truthout's 'voters slapped data centers with limits', plus analysis that the backlash may favor the biggest tech firms.

Focuses on the European protest wave, including two days of planned protests and the call to 'stop dirty data centers'. It also adds a legal and industry angle, with Pinsent Masons expecting a 'quid pro quo' on development after the US backlash.
Frames the vote as voters sending an 'unmistakable message' with data centers 'on the ballot'. The WSJ argues the backlash could play into Big Tech's hands. Fox 5 covers the rally at Schumer's home.

Frames the issue as an economic threat, with tech leaders warning the backlash endangers a trillion-dollar data centre boom. The BBC offers an explainer with 'what you need to know' ahead of the midterms.
Reports the Amsterdam incident with activists described as entering a 'building site', and the Independent quotes protesters slamming AI. It gives little other context in the items.

conflicts: Hacker News comments, US media (centrist): commenters attribute the backlash to prices or to AI generally, while Big Tech, as reported by Ars Technica, says voters' anger is 'anti-Trump' rather than 'anti-tech'.

narrative:
Coverage of the data center backlash splits into five framings, though only 24 of 140 items (17%) were framed, and agreement between coders was low (kappa 0.22, rated unreliable). The divide is therefore hard to measure.

The largest framing, at 54% of framed items (13 of 24), is European street protest and direct action. It presents the opposition as a spreading protest movement. Seattle Times, Los Angeles Times, Gadget Review, Briefs Finance, Times of India and tech-insider.org headlines fit it, mostly the Amsterdam Microsoft site entry.

Regulation, politicians and civil liberties follows at 29% (7 items). The ACLU piece and several Hacker News commenters (Grombobulous, drweevil, reasonableklout, dam_jackalopes, pj_mukh) fit it, raising regulation, NDAs and accountability.

Smaller framings:
- Business and market risk (2 items): Financial Times and Business Insider.
- Industry damage control (1 item): BankInfoSecurity, on OpenAI easing the backlash.
- Midterms as voter verdict (1 item): one Hacker News comment from ProfessorLayton.

narratives.common: The items are a scattered mix about college football and college sports rather than one single event. The clearest shared thread is routine coverage of the college football calendar, such as Week 10 schedules, CFP and AP rankings, and games and playoff storylines. Several groups only touch on college sports in general or on unrelated university and ranking news.

groups.distinct: Posts are fragmentary and span different seasons and moments: Ohio State's Big Ten expectations, Oregon and Indiana in the playoff, an AP poll alert, and the Cotton Bowl in an icy North Texas. They also cover Nebraska's 17-10 home loss to Washington, with a blog saying 'Nebraska Must Fire Matt Rhule Now', and a Romanian-language post about JD Vance dropping the CFP trophy at a White House ceremony for Ohio State. The tone is opinionated and reactive.

Commenters mention college football only in passing, using it to discuss American sports culture, school sports spending, conference realignment's effect on athletes, and college-town life. One comment proposes eliminating extracurricular sports in American schools.

Coverage is service-oriented: schedules, TV guides, games to watch, 'upset alert' picks, College GameDay locations and state-level game listings. CBS Sports frames the CFP committee's rankings through 'Anxiety Rankings', saying Notre Dame and BYU have 'no room for error'.

Items are explainers and features about the US sports system rather than weekend results: giant stadiums and ratings 'higher than the NBA', how college hockey is structured, a quarterback guide 'for dummies', and a guide to popular sports. Other items concern college basketball, with a midnight season opener and an own-basket oddity, plus a Russian regional student-sports ranking.

Football appears in political and local contexts: Masrawy profiles the first Muslim senator in America through his lacrosse and American football background. Another outlet says football stars are being used by Trump to support his party in the midterms. The rest are Egyptian university sport and ranking items, such as the African Games and a Tanta University cup.
Focus is on Moroccan angles: a Moroccan coach, Abdel Samad Tizaf, named 'Coach of the Year' in the US, plus FIFA rankings and Moroccan university league tables. No game coverage.

Reports a legal angle, a 'scandal' in which a court allows LSU to field two former NFL players, and a general overview piece on American college football. A Ukrainian basketball player's US debut also appears.

topic: Stephen Miller named chief of staff
summary: Trump named Stephen Miller White House chief of staff in place of Susie Wiles, drawing both criticism and commentary about a coming political battle.

signals.name: Stephen Miller
With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle [BBC News]
Susie Wiles

Scoop: First major White House departure as Miller takes charge [Axios]

narratives.common: President Trump announced that Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff and the architect of his immigration crackdown, will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Outlets generally tie the move to Republican losses in the midterm elections and describe Miller as a hardliner.

groups.distinct: Posts are mostly personal commentary and mockery, not reporting. They call Miller the 'architect of the brutalization of immigrants' and the 'next guy Trump pushes under the bus', compare him to Goebbels, and raise war-crimes or crimes-against-humanity accusations. Several posts drift to unrelated topics (a cat photo, a press-secretary rumor, the media ban) and add few facts about the appointment.

outlets: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
outlet_notes: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos: center-left (AI estimate)
The New York Times: center-left (AI estimate)
World Socialist Web Site: left (AI estimate)
groups.distinct: Uses strongly characterizing language: 'fiery hard-liner' (NYT), 'Hell on Earth' (Mother Jones) and a Daily Beast piece on a leaked 'sickening crackdown on free speech' plot. The LA Times says Trump is 'doubling down' after the midterm 'rout'. NBC's live updates also carry the offer of the press secretary job to UFC CEO Dana White.

Frames the move as a shift of power inside the party, with hardliners rising even though voters 'thumped' them (Politico). Axios calls Miller Trump's 'war-time consigliere' and writes of a 'Miller Doctrine'. Explainer pieces such as The Hill's '5 things to know' dominate, and the tone is more analytic than the left-leaning outlets.

Quotes Trump's explanation, 'I just wanted to make a change' (Times of India), and often uses the label 'hardliner'. Moneycontrol adds an India angle, noting Miller's past criticism of India over Russian oil and trade.

Focuses on Miller's immigration role. ABC7 Chicago ties him to 'Operation Midway Blitz', and News From The States calls him the 'mastermind' of the crackdown. ABC7 Bay Area presents 'in his words' quotes showing him as a 'bombastic critic of Democrats'. Fox 10 links the appointment to Middle East strikes. The White House page and Britannica give biographical or official profiles.

Barely discusses the appointment. Comments concern Miller's founding of America First Legal, immigration policy and enforcement debates, and a reading-list thread. One comment lists Miller alongside Trump and Hegseth with a shrug ('whatever he is').
Labels Miller the 'architect' of the immigration crackdown (Guardian) and the 'ICE architect' (Channel 4). The Independent and HuffPost UK run explainer-style pieces on who he is.
Brief, wire-style reporting using 'immigration hardliner' (FT). LBC uses the phrase 'midterms hammering'. The Economist places the story in a world news roundup next to the New Zealand election.

narrative:
Coverage of Stephen Miller replacing Susie Wiles as chief of staff splits into four framings, though only 33 of 160 items (21%) carried a framing. Reaction to midterm losses is the largest (39%). It links the change to Republican defeats, sometimes with words like "fires," "blowout" or "rout." Promotion and profile of Miller follows (33%), covering his background and the hard-line agenda. Alarm about Miller's influence (15%) quotes a former aide calling the prospect "terrifying." The neutral announcement framing is smallest (12%), though several outlets' headlines read this way.

The divide looks modest and unstable: kappa is 0.42, which the data rates "unreliable."

No outlet or account carries a political-lean label, so none can be placed on a side. By headline, WSJ, NPR, CNBC, Axios, DW, The Economist and Politico mostly used neutral announcement wording. The New York Post, The Independent, The Times of Israel, NDTV and The Times of India used midterm-loss language. The New York Times and The Telegraph leaned toward profile. Mastodon accounts split between midterm-loss and alarm posts.

Limits: outlets are judged from headlines and snippets, and each has only 2–3 items, below the thresholds for a reliable read.

summary: A gunman killed six people in Krakow's main square and three more were found at his home; Polish authorities describe him as holding far-right or ultranationalist views and the prime minister called it terrorism.

What we know so far after Krakow gun attack [BBC News]

narratives.common: A gunman opened fire in Krakow's Main Market Square in Poland on a busy Saturday, and most outlets report at least six people killed and about 15 injured. Police shot and detained the suspect, and bodies were reportedly found at his home. Officials described the suspect as holding far-right or ultranationalist views.

groups.distinct: Gives the most varied casualty figures: some headlines say 5 killed, one says 9, and counts of injured range from 12 to 16 or 'dozens'. Also stresses international reaction, with WION noting 'world leaders express solidarity', and offers explainer-style pieces ('how the attack unfolded', 'what we know so far').

Includes local-angle coverage, such as a Santa Cruz student who survived the shooting, and a US Embassy in Poland post. Quotes the minister or authorities using the label 'ultranationalistic' views. Yahoo frames the story around Poland mourning and police probing the motive. One headline says 9 killed.
The items do not discuss the shooting. They mention Kraków only in passing, in unrelated threads about buses, tech, art and labeling.
Reports the facts in a plain, wire-style way, with headlines that emphasize the toll and that bodies were found in the gunman's home. PBS gives 16 wounded, while others give 15.

Adds that two officers were wounded and that Hindustan Times named them, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, as the officers who stopped the gunman, both in critical condition. The Week links the timing to Poland's Independence Day celebrations days later.

Foregrounds the suspect's ideology, using the phrases 'far-right' gunman and 'influenced by far-right ideology', and profiles who he is. Reports that a British citizen was among the dead, and The Guardian ran a live-updates format.

outlets: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
outlet_notes: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos: center-left (AI estimate)
The New York Times: center-left (AI estimate)

narrative:
Coverage of the Krakow shooting is strongly divided by framing (kappa 0.87), with 76 of 93 items (82%) assigned a framing. Breaking-news incident reporting dominates at 62% (47 items). Headlines in this frame give casualty counts, the market-square location and police statements, and the death toll varies between five, six and nine.

Smaller framings follow:
- Far-right ideology as motive (18%, 14 items) foregrounds officials' statements that the gunman held far-right or ultranationalist views.
- Terror attack and official response (9%, 7 items) quotes police and government describing an act of terror and covers the investigation, including bodies found at the suspect's home.
- National mourning and shock (5%, 4 items) stresses grief and communal reaction.
- Eyewitness footage and personal stories (5%, 4 items) centers on video and survivor accounts.

No outlet or account carries a political-lean label. Each has only one sampled item, so the data does not show consistent leanings. Examples: CBS, BBC, Guardian, Bloomberg, ABC, PBS, NDTV, Politico, Jerusalem Post and Asharq Al-Awsat appear under incident reporting; AP under ideology; Yahoo and Reuters under mourning and shock; CNN and Euronews under footage.

Limits: outlets are judged from headlines and snippets only, and the samples are small, so these patterns are tentative.

**Briefing: ICE enforcement controversies**

Across 160 items, only 21 (13%) carried a distinct framing, and the divide is rated weak (kappa 0.69). Most coverage did not clearly adopt any frame.

Five framings appear. The most common is local-federal cooperation disputes (33%), covering 287(g) agreements and Houston's police policy. narrative:
Coverage of Trump's reported offer to Dana White of the White House press secretary job splits into four framings, with a strong divide (kappa 0.75). Of 160 items, 81 (51%) were framed.

**Framings:** The largest, at 41 items (51% of framed), is a straight announcement that Trump offered or asked White to take the role. The second, at 22 (27%), follows White's response: his plan to meet Trump, and conflicting reports that he declined or appeared to accept. A personality and spectacle angle accounts for 11 (14%), using phrases like 'please take the job'. The smallest, at 7 (9%), places the offer in a combative partisan context, citing the 'lunatic left'.

**Outlet leanings:** The data gives no political labels, only framings from single headlines. CBS News, The Washington Post, The Guardian, Bloomberg, PBS, Reuters, CNBC, NewsNation, The Telegraph and the Financial Times lean toward the straight announcement. CNN, Yahoo and The New York Times lean toward White's response. BBC and The Jerusalem Post lean toward spectacle.

**Accounts:** Most Mastodon accounts sampled post straight announcements. KimPerales and DemocracyMattersALot lean toward the combative framing, while deadline and kurtsh lean toward spectacle. lapatilla.com leans toward White's response.

**Limits:** Outlets and accounts are judged from one headline or snippet each, and all are marked as still building. Samples are small, so these placements are tentative.

groups.distinct: Posts mix OSINT-style alerts with partisan commentary. One says the IRGC claimed it attacked two tankers, one of them near the UAE coast, quoting an Iranian navy statement in Persian. Another says the vessel was running without identification or navigation systems. Others add a claimed Russian missile resupply of Iran, an unverified report of a thwarted Israeli operation before its 27 Oct election, and the line that oil traders see the war as over. One tracker counts 'Day 252' of the 'US War on Iran', and another post criticises Europe's stance.

Coverage stresses effects on India and the markets. Indiatimes reports Iran exempting Indian ships from Hormuz curbs, seen as a positive for the chemicals and pharma sectors, and BusinessLine cites an IEA warning of tight winter gas supply. Headlines also carry Trump's claim that the US is 'not at war' with Iran and that 'nobody' was hurt or killed in five months. A Riyadh early-warning alert and Qatar's mediation role also appear.

The Palestine Chronicle adds Iran's 'catastrophic' retaliation warning and Australian pressure for de-escalation.

These items focus on Trump's statements and the intra-GOP dispute. Trump is shown standing by Hegseth despite GOP criticism and pushing to restart the war, confirming new strikes near Hormuz, and insisting 'nothing is going to Iran'. OilPrice reports Hormuz shipping traffic falling while Saudi oil flows rise. National Herald says the war is 'widening'.

Coverage takes a regional-resident angle, with a Gulf News 'things UAE residents need to know' roundup. The National reports an Iranian general warning of Red Sea attacks if fighting resumes. Al Arabiya and Sout Al Emarat relay the Iranian navy's account of a single tanker striking a mine east of Hormuz and describe 'rising regional tensions'.

NDTV reports explosions on Qeshm Island after missile strikes. Other items look at Israeli politics, with Eisenkot as Netanyahu's rival forming a government and what that means for Iran and Gaza strategy. Hindustan Times casts the bounty as the US being 'desperate' for 'Mojtaba's nuclear secrets', with relocation offered to informants. An Indian Express expert piece asks whether Trump resumes the war after the midterm 'wipeout'.

Fox quotes Hegseth calling the war a 'courageous and historic effort'. WSJ describes 'clashing advisers' pressing Trump to decide on the war. The New York Post links the fresh US strikes on Iranian defences to talks over nuclear inspectors, a diplomatic angle the others mention less.

conflicts: Cause of the tanker fires: Mastodon posts quote the IRGC navy as saying it attacked two 'violating' tankers, while The Hindu, Al Arabiya and an OSINT post say the vessels hit mines.
Number of tankers: The Hindu and Mastodon's IRGC post report two tankers on fire, while Al Arabiya, Sout Al Emarat and the OSINT post describe a single tanker east of Hormuz.

Military activity: KOMO and the New York Post report Trump confirming new US strikes near Hormuz, and NDTV reports explosions on Qeshm. A Mastodon war tracker headline says oil prices fell as the 'threat of strikes recedes', and News18 quotes Trump saying the US is not at war and nobody was hurt or killed in five months.

narrative:
Coverage of the Iran war divides strongly (kappa 0.59). Of 160 items, 77 (48%) carried an identifiable framing. The largest, "Live military operations and blockade" (57%), reports strikes, the blockade, the land-route task force and mines in a mostly factual, event-by-event style. "Domestic politics and midterm fallout" follows (21%), covering GOP criticism, adviser clashes and accountability for the president and Hegseth. "Skeptical assessments of war outcomes" (10%) questions official claims, citing oil profits and reported US-Israeli failures. "Diplomacy and de-escalation tracks" (8%) centers on the Qatari plan to reopen Hormuz. "Official US triumph and resolve" is smallest (4%).

Outlet labels come only from single headlines. CBS, The Washington Post, NDTV, Reuters and Euronews fit the operations framing. The Guardian fits diplomacy. Yahoo fits domestic politics. Houston Chronicle, The Jerusalem Post and The Telegraph fit the skeptical framing. Among accounts, analytics, ScottLucas and several others post operational updates. DrALJONES, alternet and RonSupportsYou lean toward domestic politics. dailytimes.com.pk and KimPerales span two framings each.

Limits: outlets are judged from headlines and snippets, each has only one item, and account samples are small (1-4 items). The data does not support firm outlet-level conclusions.
